## 1. Scope & Inputs This cycle covers two selected Requirements for a back-end service. SDLC-FR-0302 (Record audit events) requires that every administrative action on the service is recorded as exactly one audit event containing the action, the acting identity and the time. Audit events must never contain secrets and cannot be modified or deleted through the service. SDLC-FR-0301 (Export audit events) requires that authorized users can export, as a downloadable file, every audit event whose time falls within a chosen date range, in time order, and that unauthorized export requests are refused. The normative inputs are the two Requirement trees named in the accepted Input Manifest of cycle i14-2026-10-s3. UX is recorded NOT_APPLICABLE because the selection has no user-facing surface, so no UX Document applies. Three things are out of scope because the Requirements do not define them: the set of users or roles authorized to export, which actions beyond service configuration changes count as administrative, and the export file format beyond its being downloadable. This architecture defines how the obligations are met and adds no product obligations. ## 2. Solution Structure The solution adds an audit capability inside the existing service rather than as a separate deployable. It has three layers. The first is an audit capture layer on the administrative command path. Every administrative operation, which at minimum includes every service configuration change, passes through one administrative command boundary. That boundary produces one audit event per completed action. The second is an append-only audit store in the service's primary transactional database. Audit events are written there in the same transaction as the administrative change they describe. The third is an audit export path. It exposes one export operation on the service API, enforces authorization through a pluggable export authorization policy, reads the store for the requested range in a deterministic time order, and streams the result to the caller as a downloadable file. The service has no code path that updates or deletes audit events. ## 4. Components & Responsibilities Administrative Command Boundary: the single entry point through which all administrative actions, including all service configuration changes, are executed. It establishes the acting identity from the authenticated request context and delegates the audit write to the Audit Recorder within the same unit of work. Administrative operations that bypass this boundary are not permitted by design. Audit Action Registry: a declarative list of the administrative action types the service recognises. Each action type has a stable action name and an allowlist of non-secret attributes that may be captured. The boundary refuses to run an administrative operation that has no registered action type, so new administrative operations cannot silently go unaudited. Audit Recorder: builds the audit event from the registered action name, the acting identity, a server-assigned timestamp, a server-assigned monotonically increasing sequence number and the allowlisted attributes only. It writes the event through the Audit Store's append operation. Secret Exclusion Guard: applied by the Audit Recorder. It keeps only allowlisted attributes, so free-form request payloads and credential-bearing fields are never copied into an event. It also rejects values that match the service's known secret classifications as a second line of defence. Audit Store: an append-only persistence component that offers only append and range-read operations. Export Authorization Policy: a single decision point that answers whether a given identity may export audit events. Its rule set is deliberately left open pending the product decision on who is authorized, and it denies by default. Audit Export Handler: validates the requested date range, consults the Export Authorization Policy, and refuses unauthorized requests before any data is read. For authorized requests it streams a range read from the Audit Store, in ascending timestamp then sequence order, into a downloadable file response. ## 5. Interfaces & Data Flows Recording flow: an administrative request arrives at the Administrative Command Boundary with an authenticated identity. The boundary opens a database transaction, applies the administrative change, and invokes the Audit Recorder. The recorder looks up the action in the Audit Action Registry, assembles the event with the acting identity, server time, sequence number and allowlisted attributes, and appends it to the Audit Store. The transaction then commits. Either both the change and its single audit event become durable, or neither does. A failed or rolled-back action therefore produces no event, and a completed action produces exactly one. Export flow: an authenticated caller invokes the export operation with a range start and a range end. The Audit Export Handler validates the range and asks the Export Authorization Policy for a decision. On denial it returns an authorization refusal and reads no audit data. On approval it opens a consistent read-only snapshot of the Audit Store, so events committed during the export cannot cause partial or shifting results. It then streams events whose timestamp falls within the range, ordered by timestamp with sequence number as the tie-breaker, into a file response marked for download. The file is serialized as one record per line in a self-describing text form; the Requirements leave the format open, so this is a design choice. Each record carries the action, acting identity, time and allowlisted attributes. Interface contract: the export operation takes a range, returns either a refusal or a downloadable file, and has no side effects on audit data. The store exposes no update or delete interface to any caller. ## 6. Data / Storage Audit events are stored in a dedicated append-only table in the service's primary transactional database. That database is the same one that holds the service configuration, which allows atomic writes. Each event holds an internal identifier, a monotonically increasing sequence number, a server-assigned UTC timestamp, the action name, the acting identity reference and a structured set of allowlisted non-secret attributes. An index on timestamp and sequence supports ordered range reads. Immutability is enforced at two levels. In the application, the Audit Store exposes no modify or delete operation. In the database, the service's runtime credentials hold only insert and select privileges on the audit table, so even a defect in service code cannot alter or remove events. Timestamps are stored in UTC and come from the database transaction clock, so recording and range comparison use one time base. Retention and archival are not defined by the Requirements, so no automatic purge is introduced. Storage growth is noted as a risk. ## 7. External Integrations N/A — the solution uses only the service's existing identity context and database; no external system is integrated. ## 8. Security / Authentication / Authorization Authentication: both administrative actions and export requests rely on the service's existing authentication. The acting identity recorded in an event is taken from the authenticated request context and never from caller-supplied fields, so it cannot be spoofed through request parameters. Authorization for export: one Export Authorization Policy is evaluated before any audit data is read. It denies by default, and every non-approved request receives an authorization refusal. The policy's grant rule is undefined until the product decision on authorized users or roles is made (see product questions). Integrity: database privileges remove update and delete rights from the service runtime role on the audit table, and the service exposes no mutation path. Confidentiality: the Secret Exclusion Guard keeps only allowlisted, registered attributes. Credentials, tokens, keys and free-form payloads are never captured, so an export cannot leak secrets. Export responses are served only over the service's existing encrypted transport. ## 9. Deployment / Runtime Model The audit capability runs within the existing service process and its existing deployment unit, with no new runtime component. Export is served synchronously by streaming from the database, so memory use is bounded regardless of range size. Long-running exports hold a read-only snapshot connection for their duration. Replicas of the service need no coordination, because sequence numbers and timestamps are assigned by the shared database. ## 10. Failure / Recovery If the audit append fails, the enclosing transaction rolls back and the administrative action does not take effect. An action is never applied without its event, and the caller sees the action as failed. A transaction that commits is recorded exactly once. Retries by a caller are new actions and produce their own events. An export that fails mid-stream is abandoned with no side effects, and the caller can request it again. The snapshot read guarantees that a repeated export of a fully past range returns the same content. Audit data is protected by the database's existing backup and point-in-time recovery, and restore procedures must preserve the audit table together with the configuration it describes. An unregistered administrative operation is refused at the boundary instead of running unaudited. ## 11. Observability The service emits metrics for audit events appended (by action name), audit append failures, export requests (by outcome: served, refused, invalid range, failed), export duration and exported event counts. A failed audit append is logged at error level with the action name and identity reference, never with attribute values. Authorization refusals for export are logged for security monitoring. Alerts fire on any non-zero audit append failure rate and on any administrative operation refused for missing registration, because either one signals a gap in audit coverage. ## 12. Migration Implications A new audit table and its index are added through the service's normal schema migration process. The runtime database role is granted insert and select only on that table. No historical audit data exists, so recording begins with the first administrative action after release. Existing administrative and configuration-change code paths must be routed through the Administrative Command Boundary and registered in the Audit Action Registry before release, so that no administrative action is unaudited once the capability is live. ## 13. Architecture Decisions / Trade-offs Decision 1, transactional in-database recording. Audit events are written in the same database transaction as the administrative change. This gives exactly one event per completed action and no events for failed actions, without distributed coordination. The trade-offs are that an audit store outage blocks administrative actions, which is a fail-closed choice favouring traceability over availability of administration, and that audit storage shares capacity with the primary database. Decision 2, append-only enforced at both the application and database-privilege levels. This makes modification and deletion impossible through the service even under code defects. The trade-off is that any future retention policy needs a separate, privileged mechanism outside the service. Decision 3, a single administrative command boundary with a mandatory action registry. This lets coverage of every administrative action be reasoned about and enforced: unregistered operations are refused. The trade-off is that every new administrative operation needs registration before it can run. Decision 4, allowlist capture instead of redaction. Capturing only declared non-secret attributes is safer than trying to strip secrets from arbitrary payloads. The trade-off is less forensic detail per event. Decision 5, synchronous streaming export from a consistent snapshot. This returns exactly the events of the range, in deterministic order, without a job system or temporary file storage. The trade-off is long-held connections for very large ranges. An asynchronous export would be reconsidered only if range sizes make streaming impractical. Decision 6, timestamp plus sequence ordering. Server-assigned UTC time and a monotonic sequence number give a total, stable time order even when events share a timestamp. Decision 7, a pluggable deny-by-default export authorization policy. Refusal of unauthorized requests is enforced now, while the product decision on who is authorized stays open and is not assumed. ## 14. Assumptions - The service already authenticates callers and can supply an authenticated identity for both administrative actions and export requests. - Service configuration is stored in a transactional database that can also hold the audit table, so the change and its audit event can be written atomically. - The service's database supports per-table privilege restriction and consistent read snapshots. - Audit volume over typical export ranges is small enough for synchronous streaming export to be practical. ## 15. Risks - An administrative code path that bypasses the Administrative Command Boundary would go unaudited, breaking the every-action guarantee. This is mitigated by mandatory registration and refusal of unregistered operations, but it depends on all paths being routed during migration. — Impact: HIGH - Fail-closed recording means a database or audit-write failure blocks administrative actions, reducing the availability of administration. — Impact: MEDIUM - With no defined retention, the audit table grows without bound, which may affect storage and export performance over time. — Impact: MEDIUM - Very large export ranges may hold database connections for a long time while streaming. — Impact: LOW - Until the authorized-exporter decision is made, the deny-by-default policy refuses every export, so the export capability is unusable in practice. — Impact: MEDIUM ## 16. # SDLC-FR-0301 — Export audit events

## Requirement

Authorized users can export audit events for a chosen date range as a downloadable file.

## Detailed Behavior

The export contains every audit event whose time falls within the chosen range, in time order. An export request from a user who is not authorized is refused.

## Rationale

Operators need audit evidence outside the service.

## Acceptance / Verification

An authorized user receives a file with exactly the audit events of the range; an unauthorized user receives a refusal.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

The set of users or roles authorized to export audit events is not defined by this Requirement.

## Non-Goals

Does not define the file format beyond being downloadable.

## Open Questions

None.

# SDLC-FR-0302 — Record audit events

## Requirement

Every administrative action on the service must be recorded as an audit event.

## Detailed Behavior

An audit event records the action, the acting identity and the time. Audit events cannot be modified or deleted through the service.

## Rationale

Administrative actions must be traceable.

## Acceptance / Verification

Every administrative action produces exactly one audit event.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Audit events never contain secrets.

## Non-Goals

Does not define which actions are administrative beyond service configuration changes.

## Open Questions

None.

Solution Structure The solution adds an audit capability inside the existing service rather than as a separate deployable. It has three layers. The first is an audit capture layer on the administrative command path. Every administrative operation, which at minimum includes every service configuration change, passes through one administrative command boundary. That boundary produces one audit event per completed action. The second is an append-only audit store in the service's primary transactional database. Audit events are written there in the same transaction as the administrative change they describe. The third is an audit export path. It exposes one export operation on the service API, enforces authorization through a pluggable export authorization policy, reads the store for the requested range in a deterministic time order, and streams the result to the caller as a downloadable file. The service has no code path that updates or deletes audit events. ## 4. Components & Responsibilities Administrative Command Boundary: the single entry point through which all administrative actions, including all service configuration changes, are executed. It establishes the acting identity from the authenticated request context and delegates the audit write to the Audit Recorder within the same unit of work. Administrative operations that bypass this boundary are not permitted by design. Audit Action Registry: a declarative list of the administrative action types the service recognises. Each action type has a stable action name and an allowlist of non-secret attributes that may be captured. The boundary refuses to run an administrative operation that has no registered action type, so new administrative operations cannot silently go unaudited. Audit Recorder: builds the audit event from the registered action name, the acting identity, a server-assigned timestamp, a server-assigned monotonically increasing sequence number and the allowlisted attributes only. It writes the event through the Audit Store's append operation. Secret Exclusion Guard: applied by the Audit Recorder. It keeps only allowlisted attributes, so free-form request payloads and credential-bearing fields are never copied into an event. It also rejects values that match the service's known secret classifications as a second line of defence. Audit Store: an append-only persistence component that offers only append and range-read operations. Export Authorization Policy: a single decision point that answers whether a given identity may export audit events. Its rule set is deliberately left open pending the product decision on who is authorized, and it denies by default. Audit Export Handler: validates the requested date range, consults the Export Authorization Policy, and refuses unauthorized requests before any data is read. For authorized requests it streams a range read from the Audit Store, in ascending timestamp then sequence order, into a downloadable file response. ## 5. Interfaces & Data Flows Recording flow: an administrative request arrives at the Administrative Command Boundary with an authenticated identity. The boundary opens a database transaction, applies the administrative change, and invokes the Audit Recorder. The recorder looks up the action in the Audit Action Registry, assembles the event with the acting identity, server time, sequence number and allowlisted attributes, and appends it to the Audit Store. The transaction then commits. Either both the change and its single audit event become durable, or neither does. A failed or rolled-back action therefore produces no event, and a completed action produces exactly one. Export flow: an authenticated caller invokes the export operation with a range start and a range end. The Audit Export Handler validates the range and asks the Export Authorization Policy for a decision. On denial it returns an authorization refusal and reads no audit data. On approval it opens a consistent read-only snapshot of the Audit Store, so events committed during the export cannot cause partial or shifting results. It then streams events whose timestamp falls within the range, ordered by timestamp with sequence number as the tie-breaker, into a file response marked for download. The file is serialized as one record per line in a self-describing text form; the Requirements leave the format open, so this is a design choice. Each record carries the action, acting identity, time and allowlisted attributes. Interface contract: the export operation takes a range, returns either a refusal or a downloadable file, and has no side effects on audit data. The store exposes no update or delete interface to any caller. ## 6. Data / Storage Audit events are stored in a dedicated append-only table in the service's primary transactional database. That database is the same one that holds the service configuration, which allows atomic writes. Each event holds an internal identifier, a monotonically increasing sequence number, a server-assigned UTC timestamp, the action name, the acting identity reference and a structured set of allowlisted non-secret attributes. An index on timestamp and sequence supports ordered range reads. Immutability is enforced at two levels. In the application, the Audit Store exposes no modify or delete operation. In the database, the service's runtime credentials hold only insert and select privileges on the audit table, so even a defect in service code cannot alter or remove events. Timestamps are stored in UTC and come from the database transaction clock, so recording and range comparison use one time base. Retention and archival are not defined by the Requirements, so no automatic purge is introduced. Storage growth is noted as a risk. ## 7. External Integrations N/A — the solution uses only the service's existing identity context and database; no external system is integrated. ## 8. Security / Authentication / Authorization Authentication: both administrative actions and export requests rely on the service's existing authentication. The acting identity recorded in an event is taken from the authenticated request context and never from caller-supplied fields, so it cannot be spoofed through request parameters. Authorization for export: one Export Authorization Policy is evaluated before any audit data is read. It denies by default, and every non-approved request receives an authorization refusal. The policy's grant rule is undefined until the product decision on authorized users or roles is made (see product questions). Integrity: database privileges remove update and delete rights from the service runtime role on the audit table, and the service exposes no mutation path. Confidentiality: the Secret Exclusion Guard keeps only allowlisted, registered attributes. Credentials, tokens, keys and free-form payloads are never captured, so an export cannot leak secrets. Export responses are served only over the service's existing encrypted transport. ## 9. Deployment / Runtime Model The audit capability runs within the existing service process and its existing deployment unit, with no new runtime component. Export is served synchronously by streaming from the database, so memory use is bounded regardless of range size. Long-running exports hold a read-only snapshot connection for their duration. Replicas of the service need no coordination, because sequence numbers and timestamps are assigned by the shared database. ## 10. Failure / Recovery If the audit append fails, the enclosing transaction rolls back and the administrative action does not take effect. An action is never applied without its event, and the caller sees the action as failed. A transaction that commits is recorded exactly once. Retries by a caller are new actions and produce their own events. An export that fails mid-stream is abandoned with no side effects, and the caller can request it again. The snapshot read guarantees that a repeated export of a fully past range returns the same content. Audit data is protected by the database's existing backup and point-in-time recovery, and restore procedures must preserve the audit table together with the configuration it describes. An unregistered administrative operation is refused at the boundary instead of running unaudited. ## 11. Observability The service emits metrics for audit events appended (by action name), audit append failures, export requests (by outcome: served, refused, invalid range, failed), export duration and exported event counts. A failed audit append is logged at error level with the action name and identity reference, never with attribute values. Authorization refusals for export are logged for security monitoring. Alerts fire on any non-zero audit append failure rate and on any administrative operation refused for missing registration, because either one signals a gap in audit coverage. ## 12. Migration Implications A new audit table and its index are added through the service's normal schema migration process. The runtime database role is granted insert and select only on that table. No historical audit data exists, so recording begins with the first administrative action after release. Existing administrative and configuration-change code paths must be routed through the Administrative Command Boundary and registered in the Audit Action Registry before release, so that no administrative action is unaudited once the capability is live. ## 13. Architecture Decisions / Trade-offs Decision 1, transactional in-database recording. Audit events are written in the same database transaction as the administrative change. This gives exactly one event per completed action and no events for failed actions, without distributed coordination. The trade-offs are that an audit store outage blocks administrative actions, which is a fail-closed choice favouring traceability over availability of administration, and that audit storage shares capacity with the primary database. Decision 2, append-only enforced at both the application and database-privilege levels. This makes modification and deletion impossible through the service even under code defects. The trade-off is that any future retention policy needs a separate, privileged mechanism outside the service. Decision 3, a single administrative command boundary with a mandatory action registry. This lets coverage of every administrative action be reasoned about and enforced: unregistered operations are refused. The trade-off is that every new administrative operation needs registration before it can run. Decision 4, allowlist capture instead of redaction. Capturing only declared non-secret attributes is safer than trying to strip secrets from arbitrary payloads. The trade-off is less forensic detail per event. Decision 5, synchronous streaming export from a consistent snapshot. This returns exactly the events of the range, in deterministic order, without a job system or temporary file storage. The trade-off is long-held connections for very large ranges. An asynchronous export would be reconsidered only if range sizes make streaming impractical. Decision 6, timestamp plus sequence ordering. Server-assigned UTC time and a monotonic sequence number give a total, stable time order even when events share a timestamp. Decision 7, a pluggable deny-by-default export authorization policy. Refusal of unauthorized requests is enforced now, while the product decision on who is authorized stays open and is not assumed. ## 14. Assumptions - The service already authenticates callers and can supply an authenticated identity for both administrative actions and export requests. - Service configuration is stored in a transactional database that can also hold the audit table, so the change and its audit event can be written atomically. - The service's database supports per-table privilege restriction and consistent read snapshots. - Audit volume over typical export ranges is small enough for synchronous streaming export to be practical. ## 15. Risks - An administrative code path that bypasses the Administrative Command Boundary would go unaudited, breaking the every-action guarantee. This is mitigated by mandatory registration and refusal of unregistered operations, but it depends on all paths being routed during migration. — Impact: HIGH - Fail-closed recording means a database or audit-write failure blocks administrative actions, reducing the availability of administration. — Impact: MEDIUM - With no defined retention, the audit table grows without bound, which may affect storage and export performance over time. — Impact: MEDIUM - Very large export ranges may hold database connections for a long time while streaming. — Impact: LOW - Until the authorized-exporter decision is made, the deny-by-default policy refuses every export, so the export capability is unusable in practice. — Impact: MEDIUM ## 16. assumptions: The service already authenticates callers and can supply an authenticated identity for both administrative actions and export requests.
Service configuration is stored in a transactional database that can also hold the audit table, so the change and its audit event can be written atomically.
The service's database supports per-table privilege restriction and consistent read snapshots.
Audit volume over typical export ranges is small enough for synchronous streaming export to be practical.
open_architecture_questions: Should a privileged, out-of-service archival mechanism be designed now, or deferred until a retention decision exists?
Is a maximum export range or size limit needed to keep synchronous streaming exports within operational limits, or would an asynchronous export path be warranted?

product_questions.detail: Which users or roles are authorized to export audit events? The export authorization policy cannot grant access until this is decided.
Are the start and end of the chosen date range inclusive or exclusive, and in which time zone are the dates interpreted? Exact range membership depends on this.
Which actions, beyond service configuration changes, are administrative and must be recorded? The recording mechanism is uniform, but the set of registered action types depends on this.
Is the export of audit events itself an action that must be recorded as an audit event?
Is there a retention period after which audit events may be removed outside the service, or must they be kept indefinitely?

risks.detail: An administrative code path that bypasses the Administrative Command Boundary would go unaudited, breaking the every-action guarantee. This is mitigated by mandatory registration and refusal of unregistered operations, but it depends on all paths being routed during migration.
Fail-closed recording means a database or audit-write failure blocks administrative actions, reducing the availability of administration.
With no defined retention, the audit table grows without bound, which may affect storage and export performance over time.
Very large export ranges may hold database connections for a long time while streaming.
Until the authorized-exporter decision is made, the deny-by-default policy refuses every export, so the export capability is unusable in practice.

sections.architecture_decisions: Decision 1, transactional in-database recording. Audit events are written in the same database transaction as the administrative change. This gives exactly one event per completed action and no events for failed actions, without distributed coordination. The trade-offs are that an audit store outage blocks administrative actions, which is a fail-closed choice favouring traceability over availability of administration, and that audit storage shares capacity with the primary database. Decision 2, append-only enforced at both the application and database-privilege levels. This makes modification and deletion impossible through the service even under code defects. The trade-off is that any future retention policy needs a separate, privileged mechanism outside the service. Decision 3, a single administrative command boundary with a mandatory action registry. This lets coverage of every administrative action be reasoned about and enforced: unregistered operations are refused. The trade-off is that every new administrative operation needs registration before it can run. Decision 4, allowlist capture instead of redaction. Capturing only declared non-secret attributes is safer than trying to strip secrets from arbitrary payloads. The trade-off is less forensic detail per event. Decision 5, synchronous streaming export from a consistent snapshot. This returns exactly the events of the range, in deterministic order, without a job system or temporary file storage. The trade-off is long-held connections for very large ranges. An asynchronous export would be reconsidered only if range sizes make streaming impractical. Decision 6, timestamp plus sequence ordering. Server-assigned UTC time and a monotonic sequence number give a total, stable time order even when events share a timestamp. Decision 7, a pluggable deny-by-default export authorization policy. Refusal of unauthorized requests is enforced now, while the product decision on who is authorized stays open and is not assumed.
sections.components_and_responsibilities: Administrative Command Boundary: the single entry point through which all administrative actions, including all service configuration changes, are executed. It establishes the acting identity from the authenticated request context and delegates the audit write to the Audit Recorder within the same unit of work. Administrative operations that bypass this boundary are not permitted by design. Audit Action Registry: a declarative list of the administrative action types the service recognises. Each action type has a stable action name and an allowlist of non-secret attributes that may be captured. The boundary refuses to run an administrative operation that has no registered action type, so new administrative operations cannot silently go unaudited. Audit Recorder: builds the audit event from the registered action name, the acting identity, a server-assigned timestamp, a server-assigned monotonically increasing sequence number and the allowlisted attributes only. It writes the event through the Audit Store's append operation. Secret Exclusion Guard: applied by the Audit Recorder. It keeps only allowlisted attributes, so free-form request payloads and credential-bearing fields are never copied into an event. It also rejects values that match the service's known secret classifications as a second line of defence. Audit Store: an append-only persistence component that offers only append and range-read operations. Export Authorization Policy: a single decision point that answers whether a given identity may export audit events. Its rule set is deliberately left open pending the product decision on who is authorized, and it denies by default. Audit Export Handler: validates the requested date range, consults the Export Authorization Policy, and refuses unauthorized requests before any data is read. For authorized requests it streams a range read from the Audit Store, in ascending timestamp then sequence order, into a downloadable file response.
sections.data_storage: Audit events are stored in a dedicated append-only table in the service's primary transactional database. That database is the same one that holds the service configuration, which allows atomic writes. Each event holds an internal identifier, a monotonically increasing sequence number, a server-assigned UTC timestamp, the action name, the acting identity reference and a structured set of allowlisted non-secret attributes. An index on timestamp and sequence supports ordered range reads. Immutability is enforced at two levels. In the application, the Audit Store exposes no modify or delete operation. In the database, the service's runtime credentials hold only insert and select privileges on the audit table, so even a defect in service code cannot alter or remove events. Timestamps are stored in UTC and come from the database transaction clock, so recording and range comparison use one time base. Retention and archival are not defined by the Requirements, so no automatic purge is introduced. Storage growth is noted as a risk.
sections.deployment_runtime_model: The audit capability runs within the existing service process and its existing deployment unit, with no new runtime component. Export is served synchronously by streaming from the database, so memory use is bounded regardless of range size. Long-running exports hold a read-only snapshot connection for their duration. Replicas of the service need no coordination, because sequence numbers and timestamps are assigned by the shared database.
sections.external_integrations: N/A — the solution uses only the service's existing identity context and database; no external system is integrated.
sections.failure_recovery: If the audit append fails, the enclosing transaction rolls back and the administrative action does not take effect. An action is never applied without its event, and the caller sees the action as failed. A transaction that commits is recorded exactly once. Retries by a caller are new actions and produce their own events. An export that fails mid-stream is abandoned with no side effects, and the caller can request it again. The snapshot read guarantees that a repeated export of a fully past range returns the same content. Audit data is protected by the database's existing backup and point-in-time recovery, and restore procedures must preserve the audit table together with the configuration it describes. An unregistered administrative operation is refused at the boundary instead of running unaudited.
sections.interfaces_and_data_flows: Recording flow: an administrative request arrives at the Administrative Command Boundary with an authenticated identity. The boundary opens a database transaction, applies the administrative change, and invokes the Audit Recorder. The recorder looks up the action in the Audit Action Registry, assembles the event with the acting identity, server time, sequence number and allowlisted attributes, and appends it to the Audit Store. The transaction then commits. Either both the change and its single audit event become durable, or neither does. A failed or rolled-back action therefore produces no event, and a completed action produces exactly one. Export flow: an authenticated caller invokes the export operation with a range start and a range end. The Audit Export Handler validates the range and asks the Export Authorization Policy for a decision. On denial it returns an authorization refusal and reads no audit data. On approval it opens a consistent read-only snapshot of the Audit Store, so events committed during the export cannot cause partial or shifting results. It then streams events whose timestamp falls within the range, ordered by timestamp with sequence number as the tie-breaker, into a file response marked for download. The file is serialized as one record per line in a self-describing text form; the Requirements leave the format open, so this is a design choice. Each record carries the action, acting identity, time and allowlisted attributes. Interface contract: the export operation takes a range, returns either a refusal or a downloadable file, and has no side effects on audit data. The store exposes no update or delete interface to any caller.
sections.migration_implications: A new audit table and its index are added through the service's normal schema migration process. The runtime database role is granted insert and select only on that table. No historical audit data exists, so recording begins with the first administrative action after release. Existing administrative and configuration-change code paths must be routed through the Administrative Command Boundary and registered in the Audit Action Registry before release, so that no administrative action is unaudited once the capability is live.
sections.observability: The service emits metrics for audit events appended (by action name), audit append failures, export requests (by outcome: served, refused, invalid range, failed), export duration and exported event counts. A failed audit append is logged at error level with the action name and identity reference, never with attribute values. Authorization refusals for export are logged for security monitoring. Alerts fire on any non-zero audit append failure rate and on any administrative operation refused for missing registration, because either one signals a gap in audit coverage.
sections.scope_and_inputs: This cycle covers two selected Requirements for a back-end service. SDLC-FR-0302 (Record audit events) requires that every administrative action on the service is recorded as exactly one audit event containing the action, the acting identity and the time. Audit events must never contain secrets and cannot be modified or deleted through the service. SDLC-FR-0301 (Export audit events) requires that authorized users can export, as a downloadable file, every audit event whose time falls within a chosen date range, in time order, and that unauthorized export requests are refused. The normative inputs are the two Requirement trees named in the accepted Input Manifest of cycle i14-2026-10-s3. UX is recorded NOT_APPLICABLE because the selection has no user-facing surface, so no UX Document applies. Three things are out of scope because the Requirements do not define them: the set of users or roles authorized to export, which actions beyond service configuration changes count as administrative, and the export file format beyond its being downloadable. This architecture defines how the obligations are met and adds no product obligations.
sections.security_authn_authz: Authentication: both administrative actions and export requests rely on the service's existing authentication. The acting identity recorded in an event is taken from the authenticated request context and never from caller-supplied fields, so it cannot be spoofed through request parameters. Authorization for export: one Export Authorization Policy is evaluated before any audit data is read. It denies by default, and every non-approved request receives an authorization refusal. The policy's grant rule is undefined until the product decision on authorized users or roles is made (see product questions). Integrity: database privileges remove update and delete rights from the service runtime role on the audit table, and the service exposes no mutation path. Confidentiality: the Secret Exclusion Guard keeps only allowlisted, registered attributes. Credentials, tokens, keys and free-form payloads are never captured, so an export cannot leak secrets. Export responses are served only over the service's existing encrypted transport.
sections.solution_structure: The solution adds an audit capability inside the existing service rather than as a separate deployable. It has three layers. The first is an audit capture layer on the administrative command path. Every administrative operation, which at minimum includes every service configuration change, passes through one administrative command boundary. That boundary produces one audit event per completed action. The second is an append-only audit store in the service's primary transactional database. Audit events are written there in the same transaction as the administrative change they describe. The third is an audit export path. It exposes one export operation on the service API, enforces authorization through a pluggable export authorization policy, reads the store for the requested range in a deterministic time order, and streams the result to the caller as a downloadable file. The service has no code path that updates or deletes audit events.

constraints: The set of users or roles authorized to export is not defined by the Requirement, so the authorization policy's grant rule is left open and denies by default.
The file format is not defined beyond being downloadable; the line-per-record text serialization is a design choice, not an obligation.
gaps: Who is authorized to export is undefined, so no identity can be granted export until that decision is made.
Range boundary semantics (inclusive or exclusive ends, time zone of the chosen dates) are undefined, and exact range membership depends on them.
traceability.how_satisfied: The Audit Export Handler validates the requested date range and consults a deny-by-default Export Authorization Policy before reading any data. Unauthorized requests receive a refusal. Authorized requests receive a downloadable file streamed from a consistent snapshot of the append-only Audit Store. The file contains every event whose timestamp is within the range, ordered by timestamp with sequence as the tie-breaker, so the export holds exactly the range's events in time order.

constraints: Administrative actions are defined only as including service configuration changes; any further administrative action types must be registered once identified.
Audit events never contain secrets, which is enforced through allowlist capture.
gaps: Which actions beyond service configuration changes count as administrative is undefined; the registry covers configuration changes and any other operations routed through the boundary.
traceability.how_satisfied: All administrative actions, including every service configuration change, run through a single Administrative Command Boundary. The boundary writes exactly one audit event, holding the action, the authenticated acting identity and the server time, in the same database transaction as the change. Events are written to an append-only table that has no modify or delete path in the service and no update or delete privilege for the runtime role. Only allowlisted non-secret attributes are captured, so events never contain secrets.

# SDLC-FR-0301 — Export audit events

## Requirement

Authorized users can export audit events for a chosen date range as a downloadable file.

## Detailed Behavior

The export contains every audit event whose time falls within the chosen range, in time order. An export request from a user who is not authorized is refused.

## Rationale

Operators need audit evidence outside the service.

## Acceptance / Verification

An authorized user receives a file with exactly the audit events of the range; an unauthorized user receives a refusal.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

The set of users or roles authorized to export audit events is not defined by this Requirement.

## Non-Goals

Does not define the file format beyond being downloadable.

## Open Questions

None.

# SDLC-FR-0302 — Record audit events

## Requirement

Every administrative action on the service must be recorded as an audit event.

## Detailed Behavior

An audit event records the action, the acting identity and the time. Audit events cannot be modified or deleted through the service.

## Rationale

Administrative actions must be traceable.

## Acceptance / Verification

Every administrative action produces exactly one audit event.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Audit events never contain secrets.

## Non-Goals

Does not define which actions are administrative beyond service configuration changes.

## Open Questions

None.

new_findings.detail: tsa-s06 takes event timestamps from the database transaction clock, and tsa-s05 assigns sequence numbers at insert time. Neither value follows commit order. A long-running administrative transaction can therefore commit an event with a timestamp inside a range that has already ended, after an export of that range has run. This contradicts the tsa-s10 claim that a repeated export of a fully past range returns the same content. It also leaves it unclear whether an export includes exactly the range's events, as SDLC-FR-0301 requires, or only the events committed when the snapshot was taken.

tsa-s04 says the Secret Exclusion Guard 'rejects values that match the service's known secret classifications' as a second line of defence. It does not say whether a rejection drops the attribute, fails the audit append, or rolls back the administrative action. Under the fail-closed transactional design of tsa-s10, the choice decides whether a match blocks the administrative action or still yields exactly one event. That bears on the exactly-one-event acceptance criterion of SDLC-FR-0302.

The Audit Export Handler validates the requested range before consulting the Export Authorization Policy (tsa-s04, tsa-s05). The observability outcomes in tsa-s11 list 'invalid range' separately from 'refused'. An unauthorized caller who sends an invalid range may therefore get a validation error rather than an authorization refusal. It is unclear whether that response counts as the refusal SDLC-FR-0301 requires for unauthorized requests.
